title: Distributed Caching
subtitle: Multi-instance Redis, consistent hashing, and Redis Cluster
author: KERNAL

whyItExists.problem: A single Redis node is limited by one machine's RAM and throughput. High-traffic applications may need terabytes of cache or millions of requests per second — beyond any single node.
whyItExists.solution: Distribute keys across multiple Redis nodes using consistent hashing or Redis Cluster. Each node owns a portion of the keyspace, so the cache scales horizontally.
whyItExists.whenToUse: When your dataset exceeds a single node's memory, when you need more throughput than one node can serve, or when you need high availability across data centers.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Single-node Redis handles tens of GBs and 100k+ ops/sec. Only distribute when you've exhausted vertical scaling. Cluster adds complexity — start simple.

explainModes.beginner: One Redis server can only hold so much data. Distributed caching splits the data across multiple servers, like assigning each customer to a different cashier.
explainModes.simple: Redis Cluster splits keys across multiple nodes using a hash function. The client sends each key to the right node automatically. If a node fails, Cluster can promote a replica to take over.
explainModes.standard: Redis Cluster partitions the keyspace into 16384 hash slots. Each node owns a range of slots. A key maps to a slot via CRC16(key) % 16384. The cluster client routes commands to the correct node. Replicas provide read scaling and failover.
explainModes.technical: Redis Cluster uses gossip protocol for cluster state propagation. Nodes exchange PING/PONG with partial cluster state. A node is considered failed after CLUSTER_NODE_TIMEOUT (default 15s) of no response confirmed by a majority. Slave promotion via Raft-like election. MOVED errors redirect clients to the correct node; ASK errors redirect during key migration.
explainModes.deepDive: Hash tags ({user}) allow related keys to share a slot: CRC16 uses only the content between {} as the hash input. This enables multi-key commands (MGET, pipelines) across related keys in a cluster. Without hash tags, MGET on keys hashed to different nodes would fail. Key distribution is uniform only with many keys — small key counts can produce hot slots.

content.text: A single Redis node can handle millions of ops/sec and terabytes of RAM on large hardware. But for datasets that don't fit in one machine, or for extreme throughput, you need to distribute across nodes. Redis offers two approaches: Redis Cluster (built-in) and client-side sharding.
Redis Cluster automatically shards data across nodes using 16384 hash slots. Each key is assigned a slot via CRC16(key) % 16384, and each node owns a range of slots.

content.code:
# Start 6 Redis instances (3 primary + 3 replica)
redis-server --port 7000 --cluster-enabled yes --cluster-config-file nodes-7000.conf &
redis-server --port 7001 --cluster-enabled yes --cluster-config-file nodes-7001.conf &
redis-server --port 7002 --cluster-enabled yes --cluster-config-file nodes-7002.conf &
redis-server --port 7003 --cluster-enabled yes --cluster-config-file nodes-7003.conf &
redis-server --port 7004 --cluster-enabled yes --cluster-config-file nodes-7004.conf &
redis-server --port 7005 --cluster-enabled yes --cluster-config-file nodes-7005.conf &

# Create cluster with 1 replica per primary
redis-cli --cluster create \
  127.0.0.1:7000 127.0.0.1:7001 127.0.0.1:7002 \
  127.0.0.1:7003 127.0.0.1:7004 127.0.0.1:7005 \
  --cluster-replicas 1

# Check cluster health
redis-cli -p 7000 cluster info
redis-cli -p 7000 cluster nodes

content.definition: A substring in {} in a key that Redis uses as the hash input instead of the whole key. Keys sharing the same hash tag always map to the same hash slot, enabling multi-key commands in a cluster.

content.text: For single-node deployments that need failover (but not sharding), Redis Sentinel is simpler than Cluster. It monitors a primary/replica pair and auto-promotes on failure.

content.code:
# sentinel.conf
sentinel monitor mymaster 127.0.0.1 6379 2
sentinel down-after-milliseconds mymaster 5000
sentinel failover-timeout mymaster 60000
sentinel parallel-syncs mymaster 1

a.name: Redis Cluster
a.useWhen: Dataset exceeds single-node memory or you need massive throughput

b.name: Redis Sentinel
b.useWhen: You need failover but dataset fits in one node

content.text: Redis Cluster uses 16384 hash slots distributed across shards. Use hash tags like {user:1}.name and {user:1}.email to ensure related keys land on the same shard, enabling multi-key operations.

questions.question: How many hash slots does Redis Cluster use?
questions.explanation: Redis Cluster uses exactly 16384 hash slots distributed across all primary nodes. Keys are mapped to slots via CRC16(key) % 16384.

questions.question: What is a hash tag in Redis Cluster?
options: A metadata tag added to keys
A substring in {} used to force related keys onto the same hash slot
A TTL modifier for clustered keys
questions.explanation: A hash tag is a substring between {} in a key name. Redis uses only that part as the hash input, ensuring keys with the same tag land on the same hash slot.

questions.question: What is the difference between Redis Cluster and Redis Sentinel?
options: Sentinel is for sharding, Cluster is for failover
Cluster provides both sharding and HA; Sentinel provides HA without sharding
They are identical but Sentinel is newer
questions.explanation: Redis Cluster shards data across multiple nodes AND provides failover. Redis Sentinel only provides automatic failover for a primary/replica setup without sharding.

faq.q: Can I use pipelining with Redis Cluster?
faq.a: Yes, but all keys in a pipeline must map to the same hash slot. Use hash tags {tag} in your key names to force related keys to the same slot.

faq.q: What happens when a node fails in Redis Cluster?
faq.a: Cluster detects the failure via gossip protocol, waits for CLUSTER_NODE_TIMEOUT (default 15s), then elects a replica to become the new primary via a Raft-like election.

faq.q: What is the minimum nodes for Redis Cluster?
faq.a: 3 primary nodes minimum. Each needs at least 1 replica for high availability, so 6 nodes total for a minimal HA cluster.
